doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

chapter: Coming up on the L.A. scene
title: Red Mitchell, Stan Levey and learning to practice
summary: Bass players pushed him forward; Stan Levey told him to get his technique together, so he practiced on a pad at his NBC parking-lot job, while friends Trotter, Lewis and Hutcherson later left for New York.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Absolutely. Bass players have been my — the people that have pushed me forward the most and the first that I can really remember was Red Mitchell who befriended me when I was about 17, but I already knew some other people, and I was a Jazzbo man. I went to see everybody play. And I got to meet everybody and I was hanging out at the drum shop every day. So I was on the scene and I wanted to be a part of the scene, and I was part of the scene. I just wasn’t really a good drummer but like I say I could play. But it was Stan

Levy, the great bebop drummer who befriended me and kind of essentially threatened me to become a better drummer, told me that I wasn’t — that I had a lot of possibilities but I wasn’t making it technically and I had to practice and get my hands together. And the way he said it, I don’t know if you know this about Stan but he was an ex-boxer from Philadelphia. Big guy, very brutal looking guy. He was a sweet man, a wonderful guy, but he looked at you in a way, it was like I’m going to kill you if you don’t do what I tell you to do. And I took it to heart. I said Stan — I don’t want Stan to kill me. So I got a practice pad and some big practice sticks and started practicing, you know, my ass off. And during that time I was working at, my day job was at NBC in Hollywood, I was a parking lot attendant. And I just — and we didn’t have to park cars, we’d just tell people where to go. And so we had the jazz radio on in the office and I had a practice pad with the sticks and I practiced all day at work. And you know I mean as you talk about fortuitous circumstances, you know there’s just so many. The one with my sister started dating Terry Trotter the pianist and later they got married. He introduced me to Herbie Lewis and Bobby Hutcherson who were his best pals. And I was meeting all these other people and meanwhile I’m hanging with these guys who were exceptional musicians at their age, just a year older than me, and they really liked me. And they liked me as a friend and I think they liked me as a player. I played with them a lot, up until I started really working more and everybody started leaving town and Bobby moved to New York and Herbie moved to New York and Terry got away from playing jazz, because he married my sister and they had kids.
